chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ismail ibn Marrar and others, from Yunus, from whoever narrated to him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
He was asked about a woman from whom the blood had stopped, and she did not know whether she had become pure or not.
He said: She stands upright and presses her abdomen against a wall, inserts a white piece of cotton, and raises her right leg.

So if there comes out upon the tip of the cotton something like the head of a fly of fresh blood, she has not yet become pure. But if nothing comes out, then she has indeed become pure — she should perform ghusl and pray.

key_terms.تَغْتَسِلُ: She performs ghusl — the obligatory ritual bath required after menstruation
key_terms.دَمٌ عَبِيطٌ: Fresh, bright red blood — a technical indicator of ongoing menstruation
key_terms.طَهُرَتْ: She became ritually pure (taharat) — the cessation of menstruation confirmed
key_terms.قُطْنَة بَيْضَاء: White piece of cotton — used as a physical test for the presence of blood

ai.seo_question: How does a woman in Islamic law determine if her menstrual period has ended?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) provides a precise jurisprudential ruling for determining the cessation of menstrual blood. The Imam describes a physical test using a white cotton swab: if fresh red blood appears on the tip after insertion, the woman is still in a state of ritual impurity (hayd); if no blood appears, she has become ritually pure (tahir) and must perform the obligatory ritual bath (ghusl) followed by prayer. This ruling addresses a common practical question faced by Muslim women, providing a clear physical criterion rather than relying on estimation alone.
